items.title: [cbc.ca] B.C. floods force evacuations, shelter orders as roads close
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Heavy rain and flooding across British Columbia’s South Coast prompted shelter-in-place advisories near Squamish and in Pemberton Valley, while evacuation orders covered parts of Pemberton and Lil’wat Nation on Thursday, Nov. 12. Some areas received more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours, and floodwater closed Highway 99 east of Pemberton and roads near Squamish. The entire Village of Pemberton was under an evacuation alert. Evacuation orders also remained in effect in Zeballos, where flooding and landslide risks threatened about 30 properties. The release of water from the Cheakamus Dam flooded roads near Squamish and was intended to make room in the reservoir for more rain. Officials expected river levels to crest Thursday and then recede. Rain eased in some areas, but Vancouver Island remained under rainfall and flood warnings, and forecasters were tracking more storm systems expected over the weekend.

items.title: [winnipegfreepress.com] Federal memo warns freshwater pressures threaten Canada’s long-term security
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

An internal federal memo warns that growing pressure on freshwater supplies could harm Canada’s long-term security and prosperity. It says it is unclear whether the country can meet future needs as its cities and economy grow. The Canada Water Agency prepared the document for Environment Minister Julie Dabrusin as work proceeds on a national water security strategy. Dabrusin called the strategy a “mission critical priority” in response to Prime Minister Mark Carney’s request for cabinet priorities. The memo links water risks to climate change, pollution, population growth, overuse and aging infrastructure. Public consultation ran from Sept. 9 to Oct. 25, and the agency also consulted provincial, territorial and Indigenous partners. The memo calls for an assessment of water protection and sustainable management, including shared waters with the United States and global water risks. The 12-page memo was obtained through an access-to-information request, with some material withheld.

While one population has remained stable for decades, another has declined by more than 40%, apparently due to a combination of predators, worsening storms, and changing ocean conditions. Even more surprisingly, the tiny Bounty Islands support nearly as many breeding pairs as the Antipodes Islands, despite being 40 times smaller.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says a strengthening El Niño could reach record strength by December and intensify heat and disruptive rainfall patterns into 2027. In its 2026 climate update, the agency reported that global temperatures from January through September averaged about 1.47°C above the preindustrial level and said 2026 is on track to rank among the four warmest years on record. Human-caused warming is adding to the risks associated with the naturally occurring climate pattern. The World Health Organization (WHO) has classified the expected health effects as an emergency for the first time for an El Niño event and published a plan for a Grade 3 preparedness response requiring major to maximal efforts. The agency warns that heat, drought and heavy rain can increase risks of heat illness, food insecurity and infectious disease, with vulnerable and conflict-affected communities facing particular danger. The WMO says the event is on track to reach record strength by December; its climate update uses data through September and does not include the latest impacts.

Researchers at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution plan a multiyear study of the SS United States, the retired ocean liner deliberately sunk off Florida to form an artificial reef. The project will document how a marine community develops on the ship, with initial surveys planned within the first month after its Nov. 11 sinking. The team plans to collect water samples at 132 locations around the wreck and monitor microbial communities and marine life while tracking metals — including iron, manganese and nickel — released as the steel corrodes. Researchers say the development of a reef ecosystem is seldom observed from its earliest stages. The SS United States Preservation Foundation challenged the reef’s environmental safety before the sinking. It argued that deteriorating hull coatings could release chromium and zinc and that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers had not fully assessed the environmental effects. A federal judge rejected its request to block the sinking on Nov. 6 but allowed it to refile.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Alberta bill sets data-centre limits and well cleanup funds
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Alberta introduced Bill 42 on Nov. 18, proposing new siting and water rules for large data centres and mandatory cleanup funding for every new oil and gas well. Centres using at least 10 megawatts would generally have to be at least 600 metres from homes and avoid top-quality or irrigated farmland; they would also face a near-zero cooling-water standard. The Alberta Utilities Commission would regulate the larger facilities. The province says about 30% of current proposals could be affected, while projects already far along in approvals or construction would be exempt. For new wells, companies would pay up to $50,000 initially and make equal annual payments for up to 10 years. The money would remain attached to the well if ownership changes. If a well becomes orphaned, its funding would go to the Orphan Well Association. The requirements are expected to cover wells drilled after April 1, 2027. The bill would also eliminate Alberta’s oil-sands emissions cap, which the province says is redundant with industrial carbon pricing.

items.title: [phys.org] UN warns warming will breach 1.5C as COP31 opens Monday
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The United Nations says global warming will exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius threshold as nearly 200 countries prepare to begin the COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, on Nov. 9. Climate scientists say the rate of warming has effectively doubled over the past decade. October 2026 was the hottest October on record, and 2026 is virtually certain to become the second year to exceed 1.5C, after 2024. U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said the world must now limit how far temperatures rise beyond that level and blamed political leaders for failing to act. The Nov. 9-20 talks are expected to focus on fulfilling earlier promises to move away from fossil fuels and on funding for poorer countries facing climate impacts. Turkey is promoting a goal to increase electricity’s share of global energy demand from about 20% to 35% by 2035. Developed countries have resisted further funding commitments, and the Trump administration is not taking part in negotiations.

🌲 ✏️

The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) approved construction permits on Nov. 9 for four advanced reactors at Dow’s Seadrift chemical complex on the Texas Gulf Coast, a project developed with reactor company X-energy. The units are intended to provide electricity and process heat to the site. The NRC dismissed a local environmental group’s legal challenges to the permit application.

items.title: [theglobeandmail.com] B.C. storm warnings escalate as coast faces 250 mm of rain
items.content_html:

Environment Canada escalated rainfall warnings for southwest British Columbia as a new storm system was forecast to bring more than 250 millimetres of rain to parts of Vancouver Island. Heavy rain was expected Tuesday and Wednesday, with rain continuing later in the week. Orange warnings cover west and central Vancouver Island, Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky; the provincial River Forecast Centre issued a flood watch for much of southwest B.C. The incoming storm follows weekend winds and rain that killed a driver in Surrey. Police also linked the storm to the death of a 78-year-old Vancouver pedestrian, and a canoeist is missing off northern Vancouver Island. Nearly 415,000 BC Hydro customers lost power at some point, and about 13,300 remained without electricity by late Monday afternoon. In Zeballos, evacuation orders and alerts remained in force for properties threatened by landslides. Officials expected to issue another update Friday, Nov. 13.

items.title: [euronews.com] EU auditors urge faster PFAS controls as proposed ban nears
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The European Court of Auditors warned on Nov. 18 that European Union rules and enforcement are failing to keep pace with per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), persistent chemicals used in consumer goods and industry. Its report says many PFAS remain unregistered, safety limits for food and drinking water rely on outdated evidence, and national checks are inconsistent. Restricting a substance takes an average of about 11 years, including hazard assessment and the restriction process, auditors said. Bans on individual chemicals can also prompt manufacturers to substitute related compounds with potentially similar risks. A third of EU member states reported no targeted compliance checks between 2020 and 2025. The auditors urged the European Commission to speed up a bloc-wide restriction, strengthen enforcement and revisit safety limits. The European Chemicals Agency (ECHA), the EU chemicals regulator, is expected to deliver its final assessment in December. Draft advice reported by POLITICO proposes temporary exemptions for some uses; the Commission will decide the scope of any restriction.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered Earth’s atmosphere and burned up over North Sumatra on Nov. 4, ending a nearly 22-year mission. Its observations, including millions of images, remain available for research. A 24-hour ultraviolet exposure of the Andromeda galaxy was assembled from observations made between May and July 2008. NASA said Swift detected about 20,000 ultraviolet sources there, many of them hot stars and star clusters obscured in visible-light views. Swift was designed to turn rapidly toward short-lived cosmic explosions and observe them in optical, ultraviolet and X-ray light. It also alerted other observatories so they could follow events before they faded. The U.S. Space Force said Swift reentered the atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST over North Sumatra. NASA expected most of the spacecraft to burn up, though some pieces may have survived.

items.content_html:

Full-size 3D-printed tungsten tiles survived 74 plasma discharges inside the DIII-D National Fusion Facility in San Diego, remaining intact after about four minutes of total plasma exposure over three days. The test subjected industrial-scale printed components to conditions relevant to fusion-reactor hardware, including intense heat and particle bombardment. Researchers from North Carolina State University, Oak Ridge National Laboratory and Japanese manufacturer JEOL made the tiles using electron-beam powder bed fusion, keeping the tungsten powder bed above 1,400°C during printing to limit cracking. The parts still await detailed erosion and surface analysis after a radiation survey.

items.title: [arstechnica.com] FAA plans to replace floppy-based air traffic systems by 2028
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The Federal Aviation Administration plans to replace four aging information systems that rely on floppy disks with a unified digital platform at 435 air traffic facilities by the end of 2028. The new Enterprise Information Display System, or E-IDS, will consolidate weather alerts, airport status and flight notices that controllers currently retrieve through outdated, often manual processes. The FAA says the platform will give controllers faster access to safety-critical information and reduce maintenance problems. The agency has already upgraded five sites, while Congress has provided $12.5 billion for broader air traffic control modernization. The FAA is seeking additional funding through the proposed Modern Skies Act. The agency plans to deploy the system at the remaining locations by the end of 2028.

Kyiv faced disruptions to electricity, heating and water as temperatures neared freezing, while the bridge was closed in both directions for assessment and repairs. Ukraine’s energy ministry said outages affected consumers in five regions and warned that continuing air-raid alerts were complicating repairs. items.title: [blog.ovhcloud.com] PHP hosting provider backports fixes across six million sites as patching lags
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Hosting provider OVHcloud says it deployed official fixes or its own backports across all 15 PHP versions on its shared-hosting platform, covering more than 6 million websites on about 5,000 servers. The fixes address two PHP flaws collectively known as PHP2Shell that can let attackers run commands on vulnerable servers without credentials. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has confirmed active exploitation and set an Oct. 29 deadline for federal civilian agencies to address the flaws. Censys’ tracker showed more than 10 million services patched since Oct. 21, while a scan found more than 4 million services in Germany still reporting vulnerable PHP version numbers. The scanner cautions that backported fixes may not appear in those version strings. OVHcloud says it wrote fixes for PHP 5.3 through 7.3, versions the PHP project no longer maintains. Researchers documented 35 shell executions on three deliberately vulnerable honeypots, but the test used a favorable single-worker setup. CISA has not named affected organizations or described the evidence behind its listing, and the designation does not establish the scale of successful compromises in production. Some earlier claims of successful exploitation were withdrawn or qualified after investigators found scanning or could not confirm PHP2Shell as the entry point.

items.title: [gizmodo.com] AI-driven flaw discovery strains patching as outages hit US services
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

AI tools are rapidly uncovering software vulnerabilities and helping automate cyberattacks as outages disrupt U.S. email, flight operations, banking services and an internal National Security Agency communications network. Cybersecurity experts have linked some disruptions to rushed fixes for newly found flaws, but Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said the incidents were separate operational problems and officials had no indication of malicious activity or a coordinated attack. Hackers are also using AI to automate attacks. The FBI said hackers used the Artex AI framework in attacks worldwide, with some gaining privileged access in under three hours, while Palo Alto Networks linked another framework, Cairn, to 25 operations against at least 19 organizations. Researchers also used AI to find Java4Shell, a flaw in Java’s Base64 decoding library that could let an attacker execute commands on a vulnerable server. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency urged organizations to patch it. U.S. regulators sent inquiries to banks affected by outages, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency plans a deeper review of the incidents. Canonical, the company behind Ubuntu, is separately offering AI-generated fixes to Ubuntu Pro customers through an optional early-release channel before its engineers complete normal review and testing.

items.title: [thestar.com] Supreme Court hears challenge to Canada’s ban on 2,500 firearm types
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The Supreme Court of Canada began hearing a challenge Monday to the federal ban on more than 2,500 types of firearms the government classifies as assault-style weapons. The appeal follows two lower-court defeats for gun owners, advocacy groups and businesses challenging cabinet’s authority to prohibit the guns through regulations. The ban includes some firearms used for hunting and sport shooting. The government prohibited 1,500 models and variants, including the AR-15 and Ruger Mini-14, in May 2020 and later expanded the list. Federal lawyers argue cabinet acted reasonably to address public-safety risks, while appellants say the regulations exceeded the authority Parliament granted and failed to account for lawful sporting and hunting uses. The hearings continue Tuesday, and a decision is expected by the end of 2027 at the latest. The possession amnesty runs until 90 days after the court rules.

The hearings continue Tuesday, and a decision is expected by the end of 2027 at the latest. The possession amnesty runs until 90 days after the court rules (thestar.com, theglobeandmail.com). Buyback payments: By mid-2026, Ottawa had paid businesses $96 million for about 74,000 guns, averaging roughly $1,300 per weapon (theglobeandmail.com). Ownership estimate: Federal submissions estimate that 3% to 5% of Canadian firearms owners owned firearms prohibited in 2020 and say thousands of other firearms remain available for hunting and sport shooting (ledevoir.com, nationalobserver.com). Self-represented litigants: The case has four challengers, including several people arguing without lawyers, and five other gun groups also oppose the ban (theglobeandmail.com).

Where: Ottawa, Ontario, Canada
Perspective: Canadian Coalition for Firearms Rights and other appellants: The Coalition says the regulations were too vague to fit cabinet’s powers, warning that an ambiguous standard would leave people subject to “standardless whim” (theglobeandmail.com). (The Globe and Mail)
Perspective: Alberta, Saskatchewan and Ontario: The provinces argue the federal government overstepped its powers; Alberta says hunting and shooting sports fall within provincial jurisdiction, while Ontario explicitly calls the regulations unconstitutional (The Globe and Mail)
Perspective: Canadian Coalition for Gun Control: The group supports Ottawa’s position that the Criminal Code permits cabinet to prohibit firearms by regulation, citing public safety and the ban’s consistency with the rule of law (theglobeandmail.com). (The Globe and Mail)
Quote: "Sport shooting is destroyed and hunting disrupted" (Christine Generoux, appellant, The Globe and Mail)
Timeline: October 2023: Federal Court judge rejected a challenge to the ban (nationalobserver.com).
